concepts.definition: A game is won by the team with more points when the clock reaches zero. Each basket is worth a set amount: a free throw 1 point, a field goal from inside the three-point line 2 points, and a three-pointer 3 points.
concepts.exampleLine: "Five on five, 48 minutes, most points wins."

concepts.definition: Free throws count 1, shots inside the arc 2, shots from behind the three-point line 3. A team's score is the sum of all baskets made.
concepts.exampleLine: "He was fouled on the three-pointer, so an and-one is three free throws."

concepts.definition: The boundary lines frame the court: sidelines run the length, end lines mark the baseline. Key landmarks: the half-court line, center circle, free-throw line (15 ft from the backboard), three-point arc (NBA 23 ft 9 in at top, 22 ft in corners).
concepts.exampleLine: "That three-pointer from the corner is shorter than one at the top of the key."

concepts.definition: The painted lane near the basket, 16 ft long and 12 ft wide. Players can stand in the paint for at most 3 seconds on offense. Many rules and rebounds happen here.
concepts.exampleLine: "She scored 30 points in the paint, just working the post."

concepts.definition: The arc 23 ft 9 in from the basket at the top in the NBA (22 ft in corners). Shots from behind it count 3 points. The WNBA and college arcs are closer.
A 4-ft arc under the basket where a help defender cannot draw a charge. If a help defender is in the arc, the contact is a blocking foul, not a charge.
concepts.exampleLine: "He was in the restricted area, so it was a block, not a charge."

concepts.definition: A line 15 ft from the backboard where players shoot free throws after fouls. The lane extends from here to the baseline.
concepts.exampleLine: "He is shooting from the free-throw line."

concepts.definition: The main game timer. In the NBA and WNBA, a game is 48 minutes in four 12-minute quarters (WNBA) or four 12-minute quarters (NBA); college men play 40 minutes in two 20-minute halves, college women four 10-minute quarters. The clock does not stop for fouls or the ball going out except in the last minute.
concepts.exampleLine: "Ninety-six seconds left and they are down three."

concepts.definition: A timer that limits how long a team can hold the ball before taking a shot. In the NBA and WNBA it is 24 seconds; in college 30 seconds. It resets to 14 after an offensive rebound in the NBA, but to 24 in college and the WNBA. Resetting is the shot-clock reset.
concepts.exampleLine: "Fourteen seconds left on the shot clock, they have to shoot."

concepts.definition: The NBA, WNBA and college women play in quarters (four 12-minute, 10-minute or 10-minute periods). College men play in halves (two 20-minute periods). Each has different rhythm and strategy.
concepts.exampleLine: "College is halves, so the flow is different from the NBA."

concepts.definition: An extra period (five minutes in the NBA and WNBA) played if the game is tied after regulation. Multiple overtimes are played until a winner emerges.
concepts.exampleLine: "They went to overtime and he sealed it with a three."

concepts.definition: One team's turn with the ball, ending when they take a shot, commit a turnover, or commit a foul that results in a change of possession. Possession statistics show how many times a team had the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: "We had more possessions but worse efficiency."

concepts.definition: A pass from out of bounds to start play, or to restart play after the ball goes out. The inbounder has five seconds to get the ball in play.
concepts.exampleLine: "He threw the inbound pass for a layup."

concepts.definition: A loss of possession that does not involve a shot or a foul. Turnovers include traveling, double dribble, offensive fouls, passes out of bounds, five-second violations, and steals.
concepts.exampleLine: "Three turnovers in a row killed us."

concepts.definition: At the start of the game, the referee throws the ball up and the two players nearest jump to tap it. For all other jump-ball situations, the alternating arrow points to which team gets possession; it swaps after each use.
concepts.exampleLine: "It was a jump ball but the arrow went our way."

concepts.definition: The phases of a typical possession: bring-up (getting the ball up court), half-court offense (running a set), and either a shot, turnover, or foul. Transition is the scramble when possession changes.
concepts.exampleLine: "The possession started in transition and he finished it in the post."

concepts.definition: The offensive set or system when a team is not in transition, usually run from a formation at the top of the key or with a post entry.
The scramble from one end of the court to the other after a change of possession. Transition offense is a fast attack before the defense sets; transition defense is getting back to stop it.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their transition defense is elite, nobody scores easy on the break."

concepts.definition: A guard who sets up the offense, controls the pace and initiates the ball movement. Often smaller and fast with strong passing skills.
A guard, often taller than the point guard, whose primary job is scoring from outside and hitting three-pointers.
concepts.exampleLine: "The shooting guard took over in the fourth."

concepts.definition: A forward who plays a versatile role: scoring inside and out, defending multiple positions and taking on different jobs game by game.
concepts.exampleLine: "The small forward is their best all-around player."

concepts.definition: A big man who plays closer to the basket, focusing on rebounds, interior defense and being a finisher. Increasingly asked to shoot threes.
concepts.exampleLine: "The power forward plays in the post."

concepts.definition: The tallest player on the team, usually playing near the basket on offense and defense. Responsibilities: rebounding, rim protection, and finishing close to the basket.
concepts.exampleLine: "The center is the last line of defense."

concepts.definition: A modern approach where players are defined by what they do (playmaker, shooter, defender) rather than a set position. A player may guard any opponent and play any spot on the court.
concepts.exampleLine: "Positionless basketball is how the league is heading."

concepts.definition: A guard or forward who plays on the perimeter, not in the middle. Wings are expected to shoot and defend multiple opponents.
concepts.exampleLine: "The wings are the real scorers on this team."

concepts.definition: A center or power forward; a taller player who plays near the basket and on the boards.
concepts.exampleLine: "That big can really move, he is not just a finisher."

concepts.definition: A player strong at two specific skills: making three-pointers and defending, but not a star creator or finisher. Teams build around 3-and-D wings.
concepts.exampleLine: "He is a 3-and-D guy, solid role player."

concepts.definition: A center or power forward who shoots three-pointers, spacing the floor so the inside is more open.
concepts.exampleLine: "With a stretch big, the paint is not as clogged."

concepts.definition: The best bench player, often coming off the bench to score or bring energy. The sixth-man award recognizes the top bench player each season.
concepts.exampleLine: "He won the Sixth Man Award last year."

concepts.definition: A player with a specific, defined job in the team's system: maybe shooting threes, defending tough opponents, or rebounding. Not a star, but crucial to the team.
concepts.exampleLine: "He is a role player, knows his job."

concepts.definition: A table showing each player's statistics for a game: points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks, field-goal percentage, turnovers and fouls.
concepts.exampleLine: "Look at the box score, he had a triple-double."

concepts.definition: Common basketball stats: FG (field goals), FGA (field goal attempts), FG% (field-goal percentage), 3P (three-pointers), 3PA, 3P%, FT (free throws), FTA, FT%, REB (rebounds), AST (assists), STL (steals), BLK (blocks), TO (turnovers), PF (personal fouls).
concepts.exampleLine: "His FG% and FT% are both elite."

concepts.definition: The ratio of successful shots to total shots taken, expressed as a percentage. A high FG% means efficient shooting.
concepts.exampleLine: "He is shooting fifty percent, that is elite."

concepts.definition: The point margin (positive or negative) between the teams while a player is on the court. A player with +10 means their team outscored the opponent by 10 while they played.
concepts.exampleLine: "He was plus-18 in a winning effort."

concepts.definition: Double-double: reaching double digits (10+) in two statistical categories in one game, typically points and rebounds, or points and assists. Triple-double: reaching double digits in three categories.
concepts.exampleLine: "She had a triple-double, 25 points, 12 rebounds, 11 assists."

concepts.definition: Casual conversation about a team or game, using simple concepts like positions, scores and favorite players.
concepts.exampleLine: "Did you see the game last night?"

concepts.definition: Taking more than two steps after gathering the ball without dribbling. The gather step (securing the ball) plus two more steps is allowed; a third step is a travel.
concepts.exampleLine: "That is a travel, he took four steps."

concepts.definition: The step taken while securing the ball from the dribble. After the gather, a player may take two more steps without dribbling.
concepts.exampleLine: "The gather step is the one where he catches it, then two more are legal."

concepts.definition: The foot that remains planted on the ground while a player pivots with the ball. A player with the ball can pivot by rotating on one foot, but that foot must stay in contact with the floor.
concepts.exampleLine: "He was up on his pivot foot."

concepts.definition: A move where a ball handler takes one step to one side, then a second step to the other side, evading a defender. It is legal as long as the steps are taken after the gather.
concepts.exampleLine: "He hit a euro step and got by his defender."

concepts.definition: Dribbling with both hands at the same time, or picking up the dribble and dribbling again without another player touching the ball. Both are violations.
When a dribbler palms or carries the ball (lets it rest in the palm) rather than bouncing it. Carrying is a violation and results in a turnover.
concepts.exampleLine: "He carried it, the ref called it."

concepts.definition: Bringing the ball back across half court after crossing it. A player with the ball in the front court cannot be the first to bring it back to the backcourt.
concepts.exampleLine: "Backcourt violation, he took it back across half."

concepts.definition: An offensive player spending more than three seconds in the paint while his team has the ball. The paint is the lane between the baseline and the free-throw line.
concepts.exampleLine: "Three-second call, he was in the lane too long."

concepts.definition: Two violations fall under this: (1) an inbounder has five seconds to get the ball in play; (2) a player being closely guarded has five seconds to pass or shoot.
concepts.exampleLine: "Five seconds on the inbound, they did not get it in."

concepts.definition: A team must get the ball across half court within eight seconds (ten in college). Failure to do so is a turnover.
concepts.exampleLine: "Eight-second violation, too slow getting up court."

concepts.definition: Failing to get a shot off before the shot clock expires. The ball must leave a player's hands and be heading toward the basket before time runs out.
concepts.exampleLine: "Shot-clock violation, he heaved it as time ran out."

concepts.definition: Illegal contact such as pushing, holding, elbowing or running into an opponent. Each player is allowed six personal fouls in the NBA and WNBA before fouling out; five in college.
A foul committed against a player while they are shooting. If the shot goes in, it still counts and the player gets one free throw (an and-one). If the shot misses, the player gets two free throws.
A made basket while being fouled, earning one additional free throw. The term comes from the announcer calling "and-one" after a basket is made with a foul.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got fouled on the three-pointer, so it is an and-one, three free throws."

concepts.definition: A player is disqualified from the game after receiving too many personal fouls: six in the NBA and WNBA, five in college.
concepts.exampleLine: "He fouled out with three minutes left."

concepts.definition: A non-contact foul for unsporting behavior, delay of game, arguing with the referee or other conduct violations. A technical awards the opposing team one free throw.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got a tech for complaining to the ref."

concepts.definition: Excessive or unnecessary contact that endangers an opponent's safety. A flagrant-1 is a foul with less force; flagrant-2 is excessive force and results in ejection.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a flagrant two, he got thrown out."

concepts.definition: A deliberate foul called by the referee (not based on judgment of contact) to stop play, such as a foul on an inbounder to prevent an easy score.

When a team commits a set number of fouls in a period (quarter or half), the other team is in the bonus and shoots free throws on every subsequent foul, even non-shooting fouls. NBA: bonus at five fouls per quarter; college: bonus at seven fouls per half (one-and-one) then at ten (two free throws).
concepts.exampleLine: "We are in the bonus, so every foul is two free throws."

concepts.definition: An uncontested shot from the free-throw line (15 ft from the backboard) worth one point, awarded after fouls, technical fouls, or violations.

An offensive foul when an offensive player runs into a defender who has established a legal guarding position and is not in the restricted area. The defender must be set (feet planted) before contact.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a charge, he got there first and was standing still."

concepts.definition: A foul on a defender who is not set in a legal guarding position when contact occurs, or who is sliding into the path after the ball handler has committed to their movement.
A defender standing in front of an opponent with both feet on the ground, arms up. For a charge to be called, the defender must have established this position before contact.
concepts.exampleLine: "He was in a legal guarding position, so it is a charge."

concepts.definition: A defender's right to move their arms vertically without committing a foul. A defender can move arms up and down without the defender jumping (unless they leave their feet). Contact made by a ball handler running into vertical hands is the ball handler's foul.
Touching a shot while it is on its way down toward the basket or on the rim. The basket counts automatically, and the other team gets the points.
Illegally touching the basket or backboard while a shot is in the air or after it bounces on the rim. Results in the basket counting.
A foul committed by a rebounder who leans or reaches over an opponent to get the ball without moving them first. It is a personal foul.
concepts.exampleLine: "Over the back, he jumped through him."

concepts.definition: The use of video to review certain plays (goaltending, basket interference, fouls, out-of-bounds) to make a correct call. Modern replay uses the replay center where officials review footage.
concepts.exampleLine: "They went to replay on that call."

concepts.definition: A coach can challenge one call per game (two if the first is successful). A successful challenge keeps the challenge; a failed one results in a timeout charge.
concepts.exampleLine: "He used his challenge and won it."

concepts.definition: An NBA report released after each game detailing all fouls and calls made in the final two minutes of a game or overtime, used for accountability and discussion of officiating.
concepts.exampleLine: "The L2M report showed they missed a foul call."

concepts.definition: Exaggerating or faking contact to draw a foul. Flopping is penalized with a technical foul.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a flop, he sold it hard."

concepts.definition: Hand signals used by referees to communicate calls to players, coaches, scorekeepers and fans: foul signals, traveling, double dribble, jumpball, etc.
How well players spread around the perimeter, with shooters spaced far apart to force defenders to help and leave openings for drive attacks and cutters.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their spacing opens up the lane for drives."

concepts.definition: The attention a high-volume scorer or shooter commands from the defense just by his presence. A player with gravity pulls defenders toward him, freeing teammates.
concepts.exampleLine: "His gravity opens up the offense for everyone else."

concepts.definition: A three-pointer shot from the corner, the shortest three-point distance at 22 ft in the NBA. Corner threes are highly efficient and coveted shots.
The space to the basket opened when defenders collapse to help or when spacing pulls them away. A skilled driver uses the lane to attack the rim.
A quick movement toward the basket to get open for a pass and finish. Cuts happen with or without the ball; off-ball cuts are done by a teammate without the ball.
concepts.exampleLine: "A backdoor cut got him a layup."

concepts.definition: A cut where an offensive player breaks to the basket behind a defender who is overplaying a pass. Often results in an easy layup.
concepts.exampleLine: "The backdoor cut beat their whole defense."

concepts.definition: Movement without the ball by a teammate, used to create space, set screens, or get open for a pass. Good off-ball movement spreads the defense.
A basic play where a ball handler passes to a teammate and immediately cuts to the basket for a quick return pass and layup.
concepts.exampleLine: "The give-and-go got them an easy basket."

concepts.definition: A screen set for the ball handler to help him create space or a passing lane. The ball handler uses the screen to attack the rim or create a shot.
concepts.exampleLine: "He ran a ball screen and drove to the rim."

concepts.definition: A screen set for a player without the ball to free him for a catch-and-shoot or cut. Used to get shooters open.
concepts.exampleLine: "The off-ball screen got him open for a three."

concepts.definition: Credit given to a player who sets a screen that directly leads to a basket. Modern analytics track screen assists.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got a screen assist on that basket."

concepts.definition: A screen that violates rules, such as one set by moving into a defender's path after the defender has begun moving, or one set with extended elbows or hips.
A close-range shot taken from near the basket, usually off a drive or cut. A layup bounces off the backboard and goes in.
A short-range jump shot taken from inside the three-point line but outside the paint, often used by guards to get over defenders' hands.
concepts.exampleLine: "He floated one in over the defense."

concepts.definition: A jump shot taken by a player while dribbling, pulling up to shoot mid-dribble rather than running to a set location.
Receiving a pass and immediately shooting, without dribbling. Catch-and-shoot players are often role players or specialists in perimeter shooting.
A move where an offensive player dribbles toward a defender and then steps back to create space for a jump shot.
A shot where the shooter moves away from the defender while shooting, often used by post players or mid-range specialists.
A shot where the player extends the ball away from their body in an arc, often used by post players. Less common in the modern game.
A dunk is a basket where a player jams the ball through the rim with force. An alley-oop is a pass to a teammate who dunks or lays it in mid-air.
concepts.exampleLine: "He threw an alley-oop for an easy dunk."

concepts.definition: The efficiency of a type of shot: rim (close to the basket) and three-pointers are high-quality; mid-range shots are low-quality in the modern game.
concepts.exampleLine: "They only take high-quality shots from three."

concepts.definition: A two-pointer taken from 10-22 ft, between the paint and the three-point line. Generally inefficient compared to close shots or threes.
concepts.exampleLine: "The mid-range is dead in the modern NBA."

concepts.definition: The shift in modern basketball toward taking more three-pointers and layups while avoiding mid-range shots due to efficiency.
The ratio of free throws attempted to field goals attempted for a player or team. High free-throw rates mean the team gets fouled often, a sign of attacking the rim.
concepts.exampleLine: "His free-throw rate is the highest in the league."

concepts.definition: Credit given to a player who passes to a teammate who directly scores. The official scorer awards assists; a pass leading to a basket by the scorer.
concepts.exampleLine: "He had ten assists and five turnovers."

concepts.definition: A short, quick pass (often a bounce pass) to a rolling or cutting teammate from the ball handler on a screen. Precise and efficient.
concepts.exampleLine: "Pocket pass to the roller for a layup."

concepts.definition: A long pass that skips across the court, often from one side to the opposite wing or corner to find an open shooter.
concepts.exampleLine: "Skip pass to the corner for an open three."

concepts.definition: Driving toward the rim to collapse the defense, then kicking out to an open teammate for a three. A fundamental offensive action.
Passing to a teammate who then passes to the scorer. Also called an assist-on-the-assist, not officially recorded but noticed by fans.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got the hockey assist on that play."

concepts.definition: An offensive action where a player receives the ball in the low or high post (elbow or block) with their back to the basket, and attacks from there.
concepts.exampleLine: "He posts up and scores every time."

concepts.definition: An offensive set where one player attacks their defender one-on-one while teammates stay out of the way, often with only one other person moving.
concepts.exampleLine: "Iso ball at the end of the shot clock."

concepts.definition: When a defender cannot guard their assigned opponent due to size, speed or skill difference. Offenses hunt mismatches to get easier buckets.
Two defenders guarding one offensive player, used to stop star scorers or ball handlers. Leaves another player open.
A defensive scheme where each defender is responsible for guarding one opponent, moving with that player around the court.
Defending the player who currently has the ball, trying to prevent them from scoring, passing or driving.
Playing tight on a defender's assigned opponent to make a pass to them difficult or impossible. A fundamental defensive principle.
concepts.exampleLine: "Deny him the ball, he does not get it if he does not touch it."

concepts.definition: A defender sprinting at a shooter who just received a pass, trying to close the distance and contest the shot without fouling.
A defender leaving their assigned opponent to stop a drive or penetration from another player, creating a gap in the defense.
concepts.exampleLine: "Help defense comes from the weak side."

concepts.definition: A spot on the court at the free-throw line extended, where a big man often helps on drives from the perimeter. Called the nail because it stops the drive.
The chain reaction of defenders sliding over to cover gaps after help defense leaves a player open. Good rotations stop easy buckets.
A defensive call to tell a help defender to move and cover an open player being left open by the help rotation.
The defender lowest on the court (closest to the baseline) who is responsible for the first line of help defense near the basket.
concepts.exampleLine: "The low man steps up on the drive."

concepts.definition: A defensive scheme where defenders guard areas (zones) rather than specific players. Legal since 2001 with a defensive three-second rule.
A defensive formation with two players at the top guarding the perimeter and three across the baseline guarding the paint.
concepts.exampleLine: "2-3 zone is the most common zone look."

concepts.definition: A defensive formation with three players across the top and two at the baseline, often used to protect against perimeter shooting.
concepts.exampleLine: "3-2 zone is good against three-point shooters."

concepts.definition: A defensive formation with one player at the top, three in the middle and one on the baseline, often used as a trap zone.
A hybrid zone defense that assigns each defender to guard a zone but also accounts for nearby opponents, blending zone and man-to-man principles.
concepts.exampleLine: "Matchup zone is more modern than a straight zone."

concepts.definition: A defensive formation with four defenders in a box shape around the paint, and one defender playing man-to-man on a star opponent. Used to slow down a dominant scorer.
A defender cannot spend more than three seconds in the paint without closely guarding an offensive player, even in a zone. Prevents defenders from camping in the lane.
concepts.exampleLine: "Defensive three seconds, he camped in the lane."

concepts.definition: Using your body to shield an opponent from the rebound, standing between them and the basket with your body low. A fundamental rebounding skill.
concepts.exampleLine: "Box him out so he does not get the board."

concepts.definition: A rebound grabbed by a player on the team that shot the ball. Gives the team another possession.
A rebound grabbed by the team that did not shoot the ball. Ends the other team's possession and starts a new one.
concepts.exampleLine: "Defensive rebound and push it up court."

concepts.definition: A statistic measuring the percentage of missed shots a player grabs (rebounds) when they are on the court.
concepts.exampleLine: "His rebound percentage is elite for a guard."

concepts.definition: Points scored after an offensive rebound, giving a team a second possession on the same shot attempt.
Defensive play near the basket, including shot-blocking, altering shots and discouraging drives. A core job for centers.
Defending a shot by moving a hand or arm toward the ball to distract or block the shooter, without fouling.
concepts.exampleLine: "Good shot contest, hand in their face."

concepts.definition: A defensive action where a defender swats a shot away before it reaches the basket. Blocks are tracked as a statistic.
concepts.exampleLine: "That was a sick block, he sent it into the stands."

concepts.definition: Defensive rebounding and shot-blocking in the paint, keeping opponents from scoring in the low post or getting easy layups.
concepts.exampleLine: "Paint protection is one of his strengths."

concepts.definition: A defensive action where a player takes the ball away from an opponent without it being a rebound or turnover. A highly valued defensive stat.
concepts.exampleLine: "He got three steals in the first half."

concepts.definition: A defensive action of touching a pass or shot to slightly change its path, often leading to a turnover or miss.
concepts.exampleLine: "A deflection led to a fast break."

concepts.definition: Aggressive defense applied across the entire court to trap or pressure the ball handler before half court, forcing turnovers.
concepts.exampleLine: "Full-court press to start the second half."

concepts.definition: Two defenders converging on the ball handler to force a turnover. Traps are often set near the sideline or corner.
concepts.exampleLine: "Trap him in the corner, force a turnover."

concepts.definition: Aggressively pursuing steals by leaving assigned opponents, risking getting beaten if unsuccessful. A risky defensive strategy.
concepts.exampleLine: "Too much gambling, he got beat on defense."

concepts.definition: Defensive play immediately after a change of possession, before the opponent sets up a half-court offense. Speed and communication are crucial.
concepts.exampleLine: "Transition defense was awful, they scored off every turnover."

concepts.definition: An offensive attack with numerical advantage (often three-on-two or two-on-one) before the defense can set, typically resulting in an easy basket.
A situation where the offensive team has more players near the basket than the defense, such as a three-on-two break.
concepts.exampleLine: "They had a three-on-two and scored easily."

concepts.definition: An offensive player (usually a big) who trails the fast break and arrives late to potentially catch a kickout or offensive rebound.
concepts.exampleLine: "The trailer was open for the layup."

concepts.definition: A deliberate foul on an opposing player without the ball, usually on an inbounder or someone running a fast break, to stop play. Enforcement tightened in recent years.
concepts.exampleLine: "Take foul to stop the fast break."

concepts.definition: A fundamental offensive action where a player sets a screen for the ball handler, and then moves toward the basket (rolls) or pops out for a shot.
concepts.exampleLine: "Pick-and-roll is the most run play in basketball."

concepts.definition: The player who sets a screen for the ball handler in a pick-and-roll or other screen action.
The player with the ball who initiates offensive action, often a point guard or combo guard.
The screener in a pick-and-roll who rolls (moves) toward the basket after setting the screen, often used by bigs.
concepts.exampleLine: "The roll man caught a pass in the paint."

concepts.definition: A screen where the screener pops out for a jump shot instead of rolling to the basket, often used by stretch bigs.
When the screener breaks to the basket without actually setting the screen, used to create a surprise movement.
A defensive coverage on a pick-and-roll where the screener's defender drops back toward the basket to prevent the roll, allowing the ball handler space.
A defensive technique where the screener's defender briefly steps out to slow the ball handler, then recovers back to the screener.
A defensive adjustment where two defenders trade the players they are guarding, usually in response to a screen.
An aggressive pick-and-roll coverage where two defenders converge on the ball handler immediately, trying to force a turnover.
A pick-and-roll defense where the ball handler's defender forces them to one side (icing the screen), and the screener's defender stays home.
Decisions on a pick-and-roll: go over the screen (fight through it) or go under it (around the back). The choice depends on the opponent's shooting ability.
concepts.exampleLine: "Go under because he does not shoot threes."

concepts.definition: The ability to recognize how the defense is playing a screen and react appropriately: roll, pop, pass short, shoot.
A quick pass to the screener who has moved only a short distance from the screen, before the screener's defender can recover.
concepts.exampleLine: "Short roll to the big for an open shot."

concepts.definition: A ball-handler's move to avoid using a screen by going a different direction, leaving the screener behind.
concepts.exampleLine: "Reject the screen and drive the other way."

concepts.definition: A play where the ball handler dribbles toward a teammate and hands the ball directly to them on the move.
A defender who chases an opponent receiving a dribble handoff, trying to get around the handoff spot.
concepts.exampleLine: "Chase defender got beat off the handoff."

concepts.definition: An offensive play featuring a dribble handoff or traditional handoff pass, used to create movement and quick shots.
A pass to a player in the low or high post, setting up post-up moves or actions.
A cut made by a player behind a post entry where two defenders are guarding the post player, going between them to the basket.
The area near the free-throw line extended, where a big man often receives a pass to make a play or shoot.
The corner where the free-throw line meets the lane, a key spot for shooting and passing.
concepts.exampleLine: "Catch at the elbow and make a play."

concepts.definition: A screen set for an off-ball player by another player above them on the court, often used to free a shooter.
Two screeners setting consecutive screens for an off-ball player, creating a path or opening.
A two-big screen setup where the ball handler has options to go either direction off screens set by both big men.
A screen set for an off-ball player at the three-point line, pushing them out to the perimeter.
An offensive strategy of deliberately forcing a switch to create a favorable mismatch, then attacking that mismatch.
concepts.exampleLine: "Mismatch hunting works if the big can shoot."

concepts.definition: A defensive strategy of always switching screens, preventing any mismatch opportunities but creating different vulnerabilities.
How efficiently a team scores in isolation plays, a metric showing scoring ability in one-on-one situations.
concepts.exampleLine: "Isolation efficiency is a key stat for stars."

concepts.definition: The final seconds of the shot clock, requiring quick decisions and often leading to a star's one-on-one play.
When the shot clock resets due to an offensive rebound. In the NBA it resets to 14; in college and WNBA to 24.
A late-clock desperation shot taken by the ball handler when the play breaks down or no other options are available.
concepts.exampleLine: "Bailout three to beat the shot clock."

concepts.definition: A stoppage of play called by a coach to rest players, draw up a set play, stop an opponent's run, or manage the clock.
A set play designed by a coach during a timeout, often used late in games for crucial possessions.
A series of consecutive scores by one team, often stopping with a timeout or a turnover.
concepts.exampleLine: "Stopped the momentum run with a timeout."

concepts.definition: The five players who begin a game for a team. Starters are typically the team's best players.
Which players play and how many minutes they receive. A coach's rotation is their playing-time distribution strategy.
concepts.exampleLine: "His rotation is short, only eight players get heavy minutes."

concepts.definition: A strategy of having a star sit out for part of a quarter so backup players can play, then returning refreshed.
concepts.exampleLine: "Stagger minutes to keep the star fresh."

concepts.definition: The group of backup players who play together, often forming a distinct unit with their own playing style.
Lineups with smaller, quicker players instead of traditional big men, prioritizing perimeter shooting and pace.
A lineup with two traditional centers or power forwards, emphasizing rebounding and interior defense.
The ability of players to defend different positions and sizes, necessary in modern defenses that frequently switch.
concepts.exampleLine: "Switchability is more important than traditional size now."

concepts.definition: A deliberate strategy to create favorable matchups on defense, often through switches.
An end-of-game strategy decision: whether to intentionally foul an opponent shooting a three-pointer in the final seconds.
Strategic deliberate fouls to stop the clock and reset the possession, used in tight end-game situations.
A strategy of deliberately fouling a poor free-throw shooter to send them to the line, common late in games.
concepts.exampleLine: "Hack-a-player strategy is effective but looks bad."

concepts.definition: The final possession of a quarter or game, often decided by a strategic timeout or play call.
concepts.exampleLine: "Last shot of the game for the win."

concepts.definition: A strategy of shooting with enough time remaining (usually 30+ seconds) so that your team can get one more possession in the quarter.
concepts.exampleLine: "Two-for-one strategy at the end of the half."

concepts.definition: The art of using timeouts, fouls and other strategies to control game flow and get your team's preferred possessions.
concepts.exampleLine: "Clock management in the final minute is crucial."

concepts.definition: The last chance a team has to score, often designed as a special play or isolation.
Changes a coach makes from game to game in a playoff series based on what worked and what did not.
Using fewer players in a playoff series, giving more minutes to the best players and bench players.
The benefit of playing at home, including fan support, travel rest and familiarity with the court.
concepts.exampleLine: "Home court is worth a few points."

concepts.definition: Resting healthy players to protect them from injury and maintain them for important games later.
Two games on consecutive nights, known to affect performance and rest.
An NBA rule limiting how many games star players can miss, intended to reduce load management and improve the product.
concepts.exampleLine: "The 65-game rule changes the load management calculus."

concepts.definition: The number of possessions per game, a measure of how quickly a team plays. Faster pace means more possessions and shots.
Points scored per 100 possessions, a team or player's scoring efficiency. A standard analytical measure.
Points allowed per 100 possessions, a team or player's defensive efficiency. Lower is better.
concepts.exampleLine: "Their defensive rating is the best in the league."

concepts.definition: Offensive rating minus defensive rating, a single number showing a team's overall efficiency. The most important stat.
concepts.exampleLine: "Net rating of plus-10 is championship level."

concepts.definition: Field-goal percentage adjusted so that three-pointers count as 1.5 two-pointers. Accounts for the extra value of threes.
concepts.exampleLine: "His eFG% is better than his FG% because of three-pointers."

concepts.definition: A scoring efficiency stat that accounts for field goals, three-pointers and free throws, adjusted for the number of shots taken.
A stat estimating how many points a type of play (shot, free throw, etc.) is expected to produce on average.
concepts.exampleLine: "Expected points per possession for that play is 1.2."

concepts.definition: The percentage of team possessions that end with a player taking a shot or committing a turnover. Measures how central a player is to the offense.
concepts.exampleLine: "Usage rate of 30% means he is the go-to guy."

concepts.definition: A comprehensive efficiency rating combining multiple stats into a single number. Invented by John Hollinger.
A stat allocating wins to players based on their contribution, estimating how many wins each player earned.
concepts.exampleLine: "He had 15 win shares, a big contributor."

concepts.definition: A stat estimating a player's impact on their team's point differential per 100 possessions, based on box-score numbers.
Measures how many points a player contributes over a replacement-level player across a season.
Advanced stats that combine multiple factors (offense, defense, efficiency) into a single rating, like PER or BPM.
concepts.exampleLine: "All-in-one metrics have limitations but are useful."

concepts.definition: The team's point margin when a player is on the court versus when they are off, a direct measure of their impact.
A diagram showing where players shoot from and their success rate in each area, revealing hot and cold zones.
concepts.exampleLine: "His shot chart shows he kills it from three."

concepts.definition: Shooting percentages broken down by court zones (corner three, wing, mid-range, paint), showing which areas are strongest.
concepts.exampleLine: "Zone shooting shows corner threes are his best spot."

concepts.definition: The efficiency and importance of corner three-pointers, which are shorter and often open.
concepts.exampleLine: "Corner-three value is 20% higher than wing threes."

concepts.definition: Shooting percentage from the paint, especially from the area closest to the basket.
Data from cameras tracking player and ball movement, enabling advanced stats like spacing, speed and distance.
Categorizing possessions by the type of action: isolation, pick-and-roll, post-up, transition, etc.
concepts.exampleLine: "His play-type distribution shows he isos a lot."

concepts.definition: The percentage of shots taken with a defender within a certain distance, showing how closely defended a player is.
concepts.exampleLine: "Contested shot rate of 30% means wide-open shots."

concepts.definition: A big man's ability to discourage rim attacks without necessarily getting blocks, affecting overall shot difficulty.
concepts.exampleLine: "Rim deterrence is as valuable as blocks."

concepts.definition: The debate between trusting statistics (analytics) versus the subjective evaluation of watching games (eye test).
A concept that small amounts of data (few games or shots) are not reliable predictors; larger samples are more meaningful.
concepts.exampleLine: "One hot streak is just sample-size noise."

concepts.definition: Performance in close games or crucial moments, debated whether they show true clutch ability or just randomness.
The organizational structure of the league: 30 teams in two conferences with divisions, plus playoffs and supporting tournaments.
concepts.exampleLine: "The NBA structure is complex with playoffs rewarding seeding."

concepts.definition: Teams are organized into two conferences (East and West) with three divisions each, affecting scheduling and playoff seeding.
concepts.exampleLine: "Division rivals play each other more often."

concepts.definition: The NBA plays 82 regular-season games per team, a full schedule that tests depth and consistency.
Teams ranked from one to eight in each conference based on wins and tiebreakers, determining playoff matchups.
concepts.exampleLine: "The one seed plays the eight seed."

concepts.definition: Rules used when teams have the same record: head-to-head record, division win %, conference win %, strength of schedule, net rating, etc.
concepts.exampleLine: "Tiebreaker went to them because of head-to-head."

concepts.definition: Understanding how to read and interpret the standings: wins, losses, games back and playoff implications.
concepts.exampleLine: "Reading the standings shows the playoff race."

concepts.definition: A mini tournament deciding the seventh and eighth seeds. Teams seeded 7-10 compete; 7 vs 8 is a one-and-done; 9 vs 10 winner plays loser of 7-8.
concepts.exampleLine: "Play-In games are one-and-done, so intensity is high."

concepts.definition: The first Play-In matchup between the 7th and 8th seeds, winner gets the 7 seed and loser falls to the 9/10 winner.
concepts.exampleLine: "7-8 game was epic, went to overtime."

concepts.definition: The first Play-In game between 9th and 10th seeds, winner advances to play the loser of 7 vs 8.
The NBA playoffs are four best-of-seven rounds: first round, conference semifinals, conference finals and NBA Finals.
concepts.exampleLine: "Best-of-seven means the better team usually wins."

concepts.definition: A series where the first team to win four games advances, played over a maximum of seven games.
Winning a best-of-seven series 4-0 without losing a game.
The semifinal round of the playoffs where the two remaining teams in each conference compete.
The championship series between the Eastern Conference and Western Conference champions.
An in-season tournament with group play and a knockout round, determining seeding and providing a trophy.
The opening round of the NBA Cup where teams play within their groups to advance.
concepts.exampleLine: "Group play determines the eight knockout teams."

concepts.definition: The single-elimination rounds of the NBA Cup after group play, culminating in a final.
An annual event where NBA teams select college and international players. The draft order is determined by lottery and prior-season record.
A weighted lottery determining the top 14 draft picks. The worst team gets the best odds but cannot fall below 5th.
concepts.exampleLine: "Lottery odds are weighted to discourage tanking."

concepts.definition: A team deliberately losing to improve draft position, controversial but often used by rebuilding teams.
The salary structure for drafted players determined by draft position, limiting what rookies can earn.
A contract allowing a player to split time between the NBA and the G League, earning less than a full-time NBA contract.
concepts.exampleLine: "Two-way contract is a stepping stone to the NBA."

concepts.definition: A payroll threshold set by the NBA that limits team spending. It is a soft cap with exceptions and the luxury tax.
A tax paid by teams whose payroll exceeds the luxury tax line, often exceeding $20+ million for large-market teams.
A payroll line above the luxury tax that adds restrictions: teams cannot trade for players or make mid-level exception signings.
A higher payroll line above the first apron with even stricter restrictions on trades and signings.
An NBA salary cap that teams can exceed using exceptions and Bird rights, unlike the hard cap in the NFL.
concepts.exampleLine: "Soft cap means teams can go over."

concepts.definition: The maximum salary a team can offer a free agent, set at a percentage of the salary cap.
concepts.exampleLine: "Max contract is about 35 percent of the cap."

concepts.definition: An extended maximum contract available to star players re-signing with their team, typically five years.
An exception allowing teams to sign a free agent at a level above the minimum, even if over the cap.
The right to re-sign your own free agent over the cap, named after Larry Bird. An exception to the cap.
concepts.exampleLine: "Bird rights let us keep our stars."

concepts.definition: The exchange of players' contracts between teams, subject to salary-cap rules and restrictions.
The period when players whose contracts have expired can sign with any team, usually starting in July.
concepts.exampleLine: "Free agency is wild, top stars move every year."

concepts.definition: A free agent whose team has the right to match any offer from another team or receive a draft pick.
concepts.exampleLine: "RFA gives the team a chance to keep him."

concepts.definition: A contract clause allowing a player to choose whether to play out the final year of their contract.
A contract clause allowing a team to choose whether to keep a player for the final year of their contract.
A free agent re-signing with their team and immediately being traded to another team, allowing more salary cap maneuvering.
A credit that lets a team absorb salary in a later trade without sending out matching salary.
concepts.exampleLine: "Trade exception used to get another player."

concepts.definition: A mutual agreement between a player and team to end a contract early, often in-season, allowing the player to sign elsewhere.
concepts.exampleLine: "Buyout allowed him to join a contender."

concepts.definition: The end of February, the last day teams can make trades during the regular season.
Post-season games in summer featuring rookies, G League players and young players preparing for the season.
concepts.exampleLine: "Summer league shows how rookies are developing."

concepts.definition: The schedule of events after the season: draft lottery, NBA Draft, free agency start, summer league.
Watching players without the ball to understand spacing, movement and how the offense and defense function.
The side of the court opposite the ball, where help defense often comes from and shooters hide.
The ability to see how spacing affects defense and find open spots or unguarded cutters.
concepts.exampleLine: "Spacing read led to an open cutter."

concepts.definition: An offensive set with the two bigs at the free-throw line elbows forming a "horns" shape, a popular ball-screen look.
A pick-and-roll where the ball handler uses a screen at a 45-degree angle (not at the top of the key), named after Spain's use of it.
Two off-ball screens set in sequence for a shooter, moving them up the court (like an elevator ride).
An offensive set with two big men flanking a player, creating opportunities for passes and screens.
A free-flowing offensive system with continuous movement and passing, rather than a rigid set play.
A pick-and-roll defense where the ball-handler's defender fights over the screen and the screener's defender slides to the roller.
A pick-and-roll defense where the ball-handler's defender quickly tags the roller (touches them), then recovers to the handler.
concepts.exampleLine: "Tag and recover to the ball handler."

concepts.definition: A defensive switch where defenders react late and scramble to cover new assignments, often risky.
concepts.exampleLine: "Scram switch broke down and gave up a layup."

concepts.definition: A pick-and-roll defense where the screener's defender peels off to the roller, then the ball-handler's defender recovers.
A switch executed after the screen is set, usually resulting in a mismatch or creating spacing issues.
How a single shooter or player changes spacing and assists for everyone, an advanced way to value impact.
An offensive system where a versatile big man (the hub) initiates play, creating spacing and options.
concepts.exampleLine: "Hub offense runs through the passing big."

concepts.definition: A center or power forward who excels at passing from the high post or elbow, a key part of modern offenses.
Three main pick-and-roll coverage philosophies with different trade-offs in efficiency and spacing.
concepts.exampleLine: "Drop vs switch depends on the shooters."

concepts.definition: A defensive strategy of keeping many defenders in the paint to stop drives and inside scoring.
Switching to a zone defense unexpectedly to disrupt the opponent's offensive rhythm.
The skill of creating scoring opportunities through ball-handling, footwork and spacing awareness.
Forcing defenders to collapse by threatening the rim, opening teammates.
A deceptive shooting motion without releasing the ball, used to get defenders to jump and create space.
concepts.exampleLine: "Pump fake got him airborne, easy layup."

concepts.definition: A move where a player fakes a shot to get a defender airborne, then goes around them for an easy basket.
The soft skill of finishing difficult shots, using angles and finesse rather than power.
concepts.exampleLine: "His touch around the rim is elite."

concepts.definition: The ability to quickly analyze why a possession worked or failed and communicate it clearly.
concepts.exampleLine: "Possession diagnosis shows the issue was spacing."

concepts.definition: The ongoing argument about who is the Greatest Of All Time in basketball: Jordan, LeBron, Kareem or Wilt.
concepts.exampleLine: "GOAT debate is about what you value."

concepts.definition: The central argument in GOAT debates: whether peak performance (best years) or longevity (sustained excellence) matters more.
concepts.exampleLine: "Peak vs longevity is the core debate."

concepts.definition: Adjusting player comparisons for the era they played in, accounting for rule changes, athleticism improvements and other factors.
The debate about whether championships (rings) or individual statistics are more important in evaluating greatness.
concepts.exampleLine: "Rings vs stats is a key GOAT debate."

concepts.definition: The factors voters consider for the regular-season MVP award: scoring, efficiency, team success, narrative.
The tension between what voters think (narrative) and the actual best player (value) in MVP voting.
The process of fan and media voting for MVP, All-NBA and other awards, subjective and debated.
A team built with multiple star players, often through trades or free-agent signings, designed to win championships.
The modern trend of star players having more control over their careers through free agency and trades.
Debate about whether players should stay with their teams or if leaving for other opportunities is acceptable.
The debate about whether tanking is a legitimate strategy or harmful to the league's competitive balance.
Proposed changes to the draft lottery to discourage tanking, such as weighting odds differently.
Debate about the Play-In Tournament: some love the drama, others think seeding should be based purely on wins.
The modern era of basketball where the three-pointer is prioritized over mid-range shooting.
The debate about whether the elimination of mid-range shots has improved or harmed basketball.
A controversial technique where a player exaggerates contact to draw a foul, reducing offensive play quality.
The perception that star players get preferential treatment from officials in foul calls.
concepts.exampleLine: "Star treatment is obvious in the playoffs."

concepts.definition: The gradual loosening of travel call enforcement over time, making carrying more common.
Debates about whether officiating was fair in crucial games, a permanent basketball topic.
The debate about whether "clutch" performance in close games is real or just variance.
concepts.exampleLine: "Clutch debate has stats on both sides."

concepts.definition: Using number of championships to argue a player's greatness, a simplified but popular approach.
A player known for elevated play in the playoffs compared to the regular season.
concepts.exampleLine: "Playoff performer shows up when it matters."

concepts.definition: How to disagree respectfully about basketball topics without dismissing other fans' perspectives.
Basketball was invented by Dr. James Naismith in 1891 as an indoor winter sport, first played at Springfield YMCA.
concepts.exampleLine: "Basketball started with a peach basket in 1891."

concepts.definition: The NBA was founded in 1946 as the BAA (Basketball Association of America), merging with the NBL in 1949.
The 24-second shot clock was introduced in 1954 to speed up play and make the game more exciting.
Boston Celtics won 11 championships in 13 years (1957-1969), led by Bill Russell, an NBA record.
The 1960s dominated by centers Wilt Chamberlain and Bill Russell, featuring post-centric basketball.
The historic 1980s rivalry between Lakers (Earvin "Magic" Johnson) and Celtics (Larry Bird), reviving NBA popularity.
The 1980s Lakers' fast-paced, exciting style led by Magic Johnson, contrasting with Boston's blue-collar approach.
The 1989-1990 Detroit Pistons won back-to-back championships using physical, aggressive defense.
Michael Jordan led the Chicago Bulls to six championships in eight years (1991-1998), the dynasty era.
The 1992 Olympic basketball team featuring NBA stars (Jordan, Magic, Bird, etc.), dominating internationally.
Basketball's international growth accelerated by the Dream Team and the influx of international players.
Lakers three-peat (2000-2002) with Kobe and Shaq, then the Spurs dynasty with Duncan.
The modern era (2003-present) where LeBron James has been the defining player, changing positional play and style.
The mid-2000s featured more isolation play and post-ups, less ball movement than the modern era.
The Golden State Warriors' run (2014-2019) with Curry, Durant and Thompson, revolutionizing three-point shooting.
The Warriors pioneered small-ball lineups with shooters at every position, becoming the modern template.
The gradual shift over decades to prioritize three-pointers, fully realized with the Warriors.
Amateur Athletic Union basketball is the elite youth basketball circuit, a key pipeline to college and the NBA.
College basketball players who stay only one year before declaring for the NBA Draft, common among top prospects.
The casual streetwear and fashion culture around basketball, influencing how players dress and present themselves.
The path of talented international players entering the NBA through the draft and direct signing.
Today's dominant players: Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Luka Doncic, Victor Wembanyama and others defining the game.
How basketball evolves as new generations of players bring different skills, athleticism and values.
Key differences: college plays halves (20 minutes each for men) vs NBA quarters, 30-second shot clock vs 24, five fouls vs six to foul out.
concepts.exampleLine: "College rules are different from the NBA."

concepts.definition: College men play in halves (20 minutes each), while college women, WNBA and NBA play in quarters.
College players foul out after five personal fouls, one more than the NBA/WNBA limit of six.
The day the NCAA tournament field is announced, typically the Sunday before March Madness begins.
The opening round of the NCAA tournament with four play-in games to fill the 64-team (now 68-team) bracket.
The NCAA tournament draw showing all 68 teams and matchups, which fans fill out predicting winners.
concepts.exampleLine: "Bracket is the whole March Madness experience."

concepts.definition: The round of 16 teams remaining in the NCAA tournament, played after the first weekend.
The last four teams remaining in the NCAA tournament, competing for the national championship.
concepts.exampleLine: "Final Four is the most exciting basketball."

concepts.definition: The NET (NCAA Evaluation Tool) is the primary ranking system used for NCAA tournament selection and seeding.
NCAA tournament selection considers wins by quadrant: Quad 1 (vs top-50 RPI at home), Quad 4 (vs bottom-100 away), etc.
A team on the edge of making the NCAA tournament, likely to make or miss the field based on the selection committee's decisions.
concepts.exampleLine: "Bubble team nervously waits for Selection Sunday."

concepts.definition: An automatic NCAA tournament bid awarded to the champion of each Division 1 conference.
concepts.exampleLine: "Auto bid is worth winning a conference."

concepts.definition: An NCAA tournament spot given to a team based on the selection committee's judgment, not automatic.
concepts.exampleLine: "At-large bid is for strong teams that did not win their conference."

concepts.definition: A post-season tournament won by each NCAA Division 1 conference, often an auto-bid to the NCAA tournament.
concepts.exampleLine: "Conference tournament champion gets an auto bid."

concepts.definition: A historic powerhouse college basketball program with sustained success, like Duke, North Carolina, Kansas or UCLA.
A college basketball program in a mid-tier conference, not a power conference but often competitive.
A surprising NCAA tournament run by a small-conference or low-seed team making a deep run.
Long-standing competitive and often heated matchups between college teams, carrying regional and historical significance.
The process of coaches attracting high school players to sign and play for their college program.
A high school player's verbal or written commitment to attend and play for a college program.
concepts.exampleLine: "Commitment to Duke was a big moment."

concepts.definition: The annual off-season hiring and firing of college basketball coaches, creating movement across programs.
The values, traditions and environment a coach builds in a college program, determining its identity.
The narrative arc of a college team's season from November through March Madness.
The WNBA plays a 44-game regular season (growing to 50+), single-elimination playoffs leading to a best-of-five Finals.
Best-of-three first round, best-of-five semifinals and Finals, with top two seeds getting byes.
A mid-season WNBA tournament with group play and knockout rounds, determining an additional trophy.
concepts.exampleLine: "Commissioner's Cup is a WNBA in-season tournament."

concepts.definition: Key WNBA differences from NBA: quarters are 10 minutes, ball is smaller (28.5 inches vs 29.5), three-point line closer.
The WNBA uses a 28.5-inch ball, smaller than the NBA's 29.5-inch, designed for women's hand size.
The 2026 collective bargaining agreement dramatically improved salaries and benefits for WNBA players.
The WNBA salary cap is around $7 million per team, allowing max salaries around $1.4 million for superstars.
WNBA teams carry 12 roster players plus two developmental spots, a 14-player squad.
An annual draft where WNBA teams select college and international players in order of their needs.
When a new team enters the WNBA, an expansion draft lets the new team select players from existing rosters.
concepts.exampleLine: "Expansion draft filled the new teams' rosters."

concepts.definition: Professional leagues like the EBL or international leagues where WNBA players play in their off-season.
The path from college basketball to the WNBA: draft, undrafted free agent, or international signing.
concepts.exampleLine: "College to WNBA is the dream for many."

concepts.definition: A standardized contract for WNBA rookies based on draft position, with set salary and benefits.
The growing fan base and culture of supporting WNBA teams, increasingly enthusiastic and engaged.
Current season stories and standings updated weekly, explaining what fans are talking about this week.
A preview of your team's upcoming game with context about the opponent and what to watch.
A quick explanation of the biggest current story in basketball, why fans care and what changed.
The availability statuses: Out (unavailable), Doubtful (unlikely), Questionable (uncertain), Probable (likely), or Game-time decision.
A player's availability to be determined shortly before the game, when the team decides if the player can play.
Current standings, playoff picture and how close teams are to playoff positions or the Play-In.
concepts.exampleLine: "Seeding race is tight in both conferences."

concepts.definition: Explanation of recent trades, signings or free-agent moves and their implications for teams.
Real-time updates on a playoff series: game scores, what changed and what to watch next.
Current standings in MVP, All-NBA, Rookie of the Year and other award races with commentary.
A conversational skill of asking a genuine, specific follow-up based on what someone said, showing you listened.
Responding to a tough loss with genuine empathy first, before any analysis or statistics.
Genuinely celebrating with someone when their team wins, with specific details about why they should be proud.
Admitting when you don't know something rather than bluffing with fake expertise or made-up analysis.
Participating in friendly debates about basketball topics without claiming expertise or being dismissive.
Skills for watching games in person or together: asking good questions, staying engaged, genuine reactions.
Texting during a game with genuine reactions and good questions, not fake analysis or excessive emoji.

payload.title: When they lose by 20
payload.setting: She texts after a blowout loss.

exchanges.theirMessage: I can't believe they lost by 20 at home.

replies.text: That is rough. Did they play badly or was the other team just better?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly both. Our defense was nonexistent.
replies.coachNote: Empathy + curiosity is the move.

replies.text: Well, it is just one game.
replies.coachNote: Technically true but tone-deaf when she is upset.

replies.text: I told you they were not contenders.
replies.coachNote: Never kick a fan when their team is down.

payload.closingNote: She is venting about a disappointing loss. Be a good listener.

payload.title: Load management again
payload.setting: She is frustrated about a star sitting out.

exchanges.theirMessage: He is sitting out for load management again. We need him in the playoffs.

replies.theirResponse: Yeah, and three in four nights this week.
replies.coachNote: Understanding the schedule shows you are paying attention.
Fair opinion but oversimplified.

replies.text: He is washed up if he needs rest.
replies.coachNote: Never insult a fan's favorite player.

payload.closingNote: She is nervous about losing a key player for load management in a compressed schedule.

payload.title: Cramped spacing
payload.setting: She is analyzing a bad offensive performance.

exchanges.theirMessage: Their spacing was terrible. Everyone was bunched up.

replies.text: So they had no room to attack the rim?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. The defense could help easily.
replies.coachNote: You see the consequence; that is the connection.

replies.theirResponse: Shooters spread out so the paint is open.
replies.coachNote: Asking is better than faking.

replies.theirResponse: Okay, clearly you were not watching.
replies.coachNote: Defend a core concept you do understand.

payload.closingNote: She is noticing that poor shooter placement limited their offense.

payload.title: The GOAT question

exchanges.theirMessage: Okay, top five all time. Go.

replies.text: I'll listen to your list first; I am still learning.
replies.theirResponse: Smart. Okay, Jordan, LeBron, Kareem, Wilt, Magic.
replies.coachNote: Honesty about not knowing yet is impressive.
Safe start; let her lead.
She loves this stuff; engage with it, even if lightly.

payload.closingNote: GOAT arguments are fun; there is no wrong answer, just good reasons.

payload.title: He is a hooper
payload.setting: She is impressed by a complete player.

exchanges.theirMessage: He is a real hooper. Not just a scorer.

replies.text: So he does everything—shoot, defend, pass?
replies.theirResponse: Yes! He can do it all.
replies.coachNote: You are defining the term correctly.

replies.theirResponse: A complete player. Skilled, not just a scorer.
replies.coachNote: Honest question; she will explain.
Do not dismiss her favorite type of player.

payload.closingNote: A hooper is a skilled, complete player who can play and defend anywhere on the court.

payload.title: Busted bracket
payload.setting: She is reacting to a big upset.

exchanges.theirMessage: A 15 seed just beat my 2. My bracket is dead.

replies.text: Cinderellas are the best part of the tournament. Who upset you?
replies.theirResponse: Mammoth State. I am never going to hear the end of this.
replies.coachNote: You know the magic of upsets.

replies.text: That is what you get for picking chalk.
replies.coachNote: True but not comforting.
Upsets happen; do not blame the system.

payload.closingNote: She picked a high seed that lost early. Cinderellas (big underdogs) make March Madness special.

payload.title: Can't defend the switch
payload.setting: She is frustrated with defensive breakdowns.

exchanges.theirMessage: Their bigs can switch onto guards and hunt mismatches. We cannot stop it.

replies.text: So when they switch, a big ends up on a small guy who can drive?
replies.theirResponse: Exactly. We get torched in the mid-range and drive.
replies.coachNote: You see how the mismatch works.

replies.theirResponse: When a defender switches onto a different opponent.
replies.coachNote: Good question; it is important.
Oversimplification does not help.

payload.closingNote: She is talking about a defensive scheme (switching) that exposes her team's weaknesses.

payload.title: Playoff night in the W
payload.setting: She is excited about a WNBA playoff win.

exchanges.theirMessage: Did you see the Sparks close that one out?? Elite fourth quarter!

replies.text: I missed it but I heard it was tight. Who sealed it?
